sections.title: Batching: static vs continuous, and the throughput math

In-flight batching: finished requests leave, new ones join at every decode step.

recall.question: Why does continuous batching matter?
recall.answer: Decode is memory-bandwidth bound; one streaming pass costs nearly the same for 1 or many sequences.

sections.title: The KV cache: where decode's cost lives

keyTerms.definition: Saved keys and values per token; turns quadratic recompute into flat per-step append.
Naive recompute grows with the square of answer length.

recall.question: What does the cache save?
recall.answer: Recomputing all previous keys and values on every step; step 1000 re-reads 999 tokens naively.

sections.title: KV cache paging and disaggregated prefill/decode

keyTerms.definition: Manages the KV cache like an OS manages RAM: fixed blocks, block tables.
Dead memory between actual and reserved length; caps batch size.
Splits prefill and decode phases.

recall.question: Why does paging exist?
recall.answer: Plain contiguous allocation reserves each sequence's max length up front; the gap is dead memory.

sections.title: Quantization survey: PTQ, GGUF , QAT , and what breaks

keyTerms.definition: Fewer bits per number: fp16 to int8 to int4; the cheapest big lever in serving.

recall.question: Why is quantization the cheapest lever?
recall.answer: Decode is memory-bound; halving bytes nearly halves cost per token and doubles the fitting batch.

recall.question: How much does a 70B model need?
recall.answer: 140 GB in fp16 (two A100 80GB); 35 GB in int4 (one card).

keyTerms.definition: Small draft model guesses ahead; big model verifies in one pass.

recall.question: Why does the output match the big model alone?
recall.answer: Every kept token passed the target's own verification; the first disagreement gets fixed.

recall.question: When does it pay?
recall.answer: When the draft is right most of the time: several expensive passes become one plus a few cheap ones.
